findings.original: Every digital circuit, from a light switch to a CPU core, computes functions whose inputs and outputs are only ever 0 or 1.
findings.correction: Boolean algebra models binary signals with values 0 and 1. Physical digital circuits use voltage ranges, have transition intervals and may encounter unknown, metastable or high-impedance states; sequential circuits also depend on stored state.

findings.original: In silicon, electrons (which carry current in nMOS) are roughly two to three times more mobile than holes (which carry it in pMOS). A pMOS must be made wider to switch as fast as an nMOS of the same size.
findings.correction: In conventional silicon design models, nMOS often has greater drive strength than a comparably sized pMOS. Designers commonly widen pMOS devices to balance rise and fall times; the ratio depends on process, device geometry and operating point.

findings.original: For the same speed, a NAND is smaller, so designers prefer NAND and keep NOR gates narrow. Series stacks of more than about four transistors are generally avoided altogether; wide functions are built as trees of smaller gates.
findings.correction: In the conventional sizing model, balancing a wide NOR can cost more area and input capacitance than a NAND. Real choices depend on the cell library and load. Deep series stacks increase resistance, so wide functions are often factored into smaller gates; there is no universal four-device cutoff.

findings.original: The time from an input change to the output settling is the **propagation delay**, around ten picoseconds for a simple gate in a modern process.
findings.correction:
Propagation delay characterises the input-to-output response under specified thresholds, load, slew, process, voltage and temperature. A timing model may bound the time until a valid output.

> [!note] Evidence gap
> A universal modern-gate delay is omitted because no process, library cell, load or operating corner was supplied to verify the previous ten-picosecond figure.

findings.correction: Equivalent two-level AND-OR and NAND-NAND designs can have the same number of logic boxes but different transistor counts and delays. Compare actual cells, fan-in, loading and wiring.

findings.original: A single CMOS stage is inverting, so NAND and NOR (4 transistors) are cheaper than AND and OR (6). NAND is preferred over NOR because slow pMOS transistors end up in parallel.
findings.correction: In the conventional fully complementary construction, NAND2/NOR2 use four transistors; adding an inverter gives six-transistor AND2/OR2. NAND often has a favourable sizing tradeoff, depending on library and load.

findings.original: FF_a may go metastable, but it has a whole clock cycle to resolve before FF_b samples it. The chance that it is still unresolved by then is tiny, giving a mean time between failures of years or more for typical designs.
findings.correction:
FF_a may go metastable. Resolution time is roughly a cycle minus stage, routing and setup overhead; placement matters. The failure rate depends on device parameters, clock frequency and asynchronous transition rate, so stage count must be justified against the required MTBF.

> [!note] Evidence gap
> A generic years-long MTBF is omitted because the required device and timing parameters were unavailable. A two-stage chain reduces risk but does not prove an acceptable failure rate.

A short pulse can be missed entirely; use pulse stretching or an appropriate handshake/toggle protocol when every event must be transferred. A push-button also requires debouncing separately.

findings.correction: **Moore machine**: outputs depend only on state. In a synchronous model, an input affects them after a state update. Combinational decoding of state bits can glitch during transitions as bits arrive at different times; register the output or design a suitable hazard-free encoding when needed. The latency comparison with Mealy depends on when inputs and outputs are sampled.

findings.original: DDR4 requires each row to be refreshed within **64 ms** at normal temperatures (32 ms when hot); DDR5 halves the window to 32 ms. The memory controller spreads this out by issuing a refresh command roughly every 7.8 µs for DDR4 (8,192 commands per 64 ms), during which the affected memory cannot serve requests.
findings.correction:
Refresh windows and commands depend on the device, temperature and selected refresh mode. As an illustrative schedule, 8,192 refresh operations in a 64 ms window average 7.8125 microseconds apart. Controllers must obey the part's timing and scheduling limits; affected banks cannot serve ordinary accesses during their refresh operation.

> [!note] Evidence gap
> A blanket DDR4/DDR5 refresh-window rule is omitted because no complete part-specific temperature/mode table was verified for that claim. Use the selected device's datasheet; the arithmetic example is not a controller specification.

findings.original: SRAM is a 6T bistable cell: fast, static, large, used for registers and caches. DRAM is 1T1C: dense and cheap, but reads are destructive, rows must be refreshed (within 64 ms for DDR4, 32 ms for DDR5), and it lives off-chip.
findings.correction: The illustrated SRAM cell is 6T and the DRAM cell is 1T1C. SRAM holds while powered without periodic refresh; DRAM activation disturbs charge and restores it, and refresh follows device-specific requirements. Other cell variants and embedded DRAM exist.

findings.original: Being a Moore machine, Z changes only at edges, one cycle after the second 1 arrives.
findings.correction: Here Z is a state bit and becomes 1 after the edge sampling the second consecutive 1. It does not wait another full cycle after that edge; arbitrary decoded Moore outputs can also glitch during state transitions.

findings.question: logic-sequential-q9
findings.original: The 6 unused codes (10 to 15) are don't-cares for the next-state logic, which helps minimisation, but a robust design should still send them back to a known state.
findings.correction: The six unused codes may be treated as don't-cares only under an invariant excluding them. If recovery is required, specify and verify it instead; a don't-care does not promise any recovery transition.

findings.question: logic-sequential-q12
findings.original: A short pulse on D while CLK = 1 has no effect on Q
findings.correction: A pulse wholly within CLK = 1, away from capture timing windows, has no effect on Q in the ideal model

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q2
findings.original: DDR4 requires every row to be refreshed within 64 ms.
findings.correction: The permitted window depends on the selected device, temperature and refresh mode; use its datasheet.

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q6
findings.original: store x7 to address x6 + 8
findings.correction: store the low 32 bits of x7 to address x6 + 8

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q6
findings.original: would write garbage into the rd field's register.
findings.correction: would incorrectly write a register selected from instruction bits; RISC-V stores have no rd field (those bit positions hold immediate bits).

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q7
findings.original: further reads from that same row are faster than reads from a different row
findings.correction: a read can avoid activation/precharge overhead compared with accessing a conflicting row in the same bank

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q7
findings.original: the sense amplifier restores it as part of every read.
findings.correction: activation senses and restores the row; subsequent column reads from the open row use the row buffer.

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q7
findings.original: refresh   never         <= 64 ms
findings.correction: refresh   not required  device-specific

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q8
findings.original: Muxes are negligible.
findings.correction: This toy load/store subset assumes no other instruction is slower, and mux, launch clock-to-Q, wire, skew and jitter contributions are negligible.

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q9
findings.original: which is DDR4's nominal refresh interval at normal temperature.
findings.correction: for the stipulated illustrative schedule; actual device modes and temperature limits must be checked.

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q9
findings.original: Above about 85 °C cells leak faster and the window halves to 32 ms, so commands come every 3.9 µs, costing more bandwidth.
findings.correction: If the selected device and mode require the same command count in a 32 ms window, the mean interval becomes 3.90625 microseconds. Temperature thresholds must come from that device's datasheet.

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q10
findings.original: // case ... default: y = 'bx;
findings.correction: // use a defined default for valid inputs
findings.reason: X is synthesis don't-care, not a safe output value.

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q11
findings.original: Without the `default` branch, a stray `state` of 11 would leave `next` unassigned, and synthesis would infer a latch
findings.correction: Without the default branch, RTL simulation at state 11 leaves next unassigned, creating unintended retention semantics

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q11
findings.original: True. With no default, the case does not cover 11, so `next` must hold its value on that path, which is a latch. The default also gives a recovery path from an illegal state.
findings.correction: True for RTL simulation: next retains its previous value on that path. Generic synthesis can infer a latch, but FSM extraction and unreachable-state optimization may transform it. A default supplies RTL recovery; physical recovery requires checking the synthesized FSM.

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q11
findings.original: so it changes only at clock edges.
findings.correction: so it is Moore. Decoding state bits can glitch during transitions; the definition alone does not guarantee a glitch-free physical output.

findings.question: logic-datapath-memory-q12
findings.original: being an order of magnitude or more faster and sitting on the CPU die.
findings.correction: providing low-latency access near the core; the ratio depends on cache level, size, DRAM row state and the complete memory path.
